title: Why Flowers Pay Insects To Travel
text:
A plant has a problem that an animal does not: it cannot move in order to find a mate. Pollen must somehow reach the stigma of another individual, and since pollinating itself narrows the genetic variation a population can draw on, plants have to move their gametes by some external means. Wind is one answer, and grasses and many northern trees rely on it, but wind is indiscriminate. A plant using it must produce pollen in enormous quantities and accept that almost all of it will land somewhere useless.

The alternative is to hire a courier. Flowers evolved as advertisements, offering colour, scent, a particular shape, and a reward of nectar or surplus pollen, and an insect that visits one flower and then another of the same species delivers pollen exactly where it is wanted. That precision means far less pollen is needed. It also creates a mutual dependence, sometimes an extreme one: certain orchids are pollinated by a single insect species, and a flower shaped to admit only one visitor is efficient until that visitor becomes scarce. What looks like decoration, then, is a solution to a reproductive constraint, and the variety of flower form largely mirrors the variety of animals being recruited.
points: A plant cannot move to find a mate, so its pollen must be carried to another individual.
Self-pollination narrows genetic variation, so plants need an external means of transferring gametes.
Wind pollination works but is indiscriminate, requiring huge quantities of pollen that is mostly wasted.
Flowers advertise with colour, scent, shape and rewards such as nectar in order to recruit animal pollinators.
An animal carrying pollen between flowers of the same species is far more precise, so much less pollen is needed.
This creates mutual dependence, sometimes on a single species, which is a risk, and flower diversity reflects pollinator diversity.
